package_info.package_versions: unknown (all versions published to public npm registry by attacker)
package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it is a namespace-squatting attack: an attacker published a package named 'piedpiper-middle-out'—matching a proprietary internal package—to the public npm registry. This can deceive organizations into installing the attacker's code instead of their legitimate internal package, resulting in potential code execution, data exfiltration, or other supply chain attacks.

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when the package is required or loaded by an application)
execution_context.file_location: index.js (main entry point of the malicious npm package)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code reads the SECRET_TOKEN environment variable and the contents of /etc/passwd, then sends this data via HTTPS POST to attacker.example.com, resulting in credential and system information exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code immediately accesses sensitive environment variables and system files upon import, then transmits this data to an external, attacker-controlled domain. This is a direct exfiltration technique commonly used in supply chain attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate package with this name should only provide the expected business logic and should not access sensitive files or environment variables, nor communicate with unknown external domains. Such data access and exfiltration is not expected in a business library.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may read environment variables or configuration files for setup, but should never transmit their contents to untrusted or undocumented external domains.
key_indicators: Access to sensitive files such as /etc/passwd
Outbound HTTPS POST requests to attacker.example.com
Data exfiltration logic present in the main entry point (index.js)
No legitimate documentation or business logic justifying this data flow

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes a malicious package named 'piedpiper-middle-out' to the public npm registry, matching the name of a proprietary internal package.
attack_chain.leads_to: Developers or automated systems may inadvertently install the malicious public package instead of the intended internal one.

attack_chain.action: A developer or CI/CD pipeline installs the malicious package from the public npm registry.
attack_chain.leads_to: The malicious code within the package is executed during import-time.

attack_chain.action: The malicious code executes, harvesting environment variables and sensitive files, then exfiltrates this data to the attacker's server.
attack_chain.leads_to: The attacker gains access to sensitive credentials and system information from the compromised environment.

behavioral_signatures: Package published to a public registry with a name matching known internal or proprietary libraries
Unexpected network requests to untrusted domains (e.g., attacker.example.com) during package import or runtime
Access to sensitive files (such as /etc/passwd) or environment variables (e.g., SECRET_TOKEN) not documented in package usage
file_indicators: index.js or main entry point containing code that reads environment variables and system files
Hardcoded references to external domains (e.g., attacker.example.com) within package source code
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS POST requests to domains not associated with the organization, specifically attacker.example.com
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure during package import or runtime
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for installation of packages from public registries that match the names of internal or proprietary packages. Analyze package contents for code that accesses sensitive files or environment variables and makes outbound network requests to untrusted domains. Use repository routing rules to block requests for internal package names from public registries. Implement network monitoring to detect suspicious exfiltration attempts from build or runtime environments, and scan for hardcoded external domains in package source code.
